entries.title: Menu French a server says
entries.summary: The few dozen French words an American menu still carries: the little joining words, the course names, the ways a meal is priced, and the sauce and cooking words guests ask about. Say each simply, then in plain English.
entries.guest: En papillote just means in paper: the fish is sealed in a parcel, here a banana leaf, so it steams in its own juices and stays moist.

paras: Menu French is the small set of French words American menus still use: joining words, course names, ways of pricing a meal, and the sauce and cooking words guests ask about. You need no French, just a few dozen words said clearly, with the plain meaning ready behind each.

The little words tell you how to read the rest. À la (ah LAH) means in the style of: à la Créole is the Creole way. Au and aux (both OH) mean with: au jus is with its juice. En (AHN) means in: en croûte, in pastry. Sur (SOOR) means on, and de (DUH) means of: pot de crème, literally a pot of cream, is a baked custard set in a little pot. In a long name the main ingredient usually comes first, and the little word says what comes with it or how it is cooked.

The course words follow the meal. An amuse-bouche (ah-mooz BOOSH), a mouth amuser, is one bite the chef sends before the meal, neither ordered nor charged. Hors d'oeuvre (or DURV), literally outside the work, means small savoury bites served apart from the meal. Entrée (AHN-tray) is the trap. In nineteenth-century French dinners it was a substantial dish served before the roast; American menus kept it for the main course, while in France today it means the starter, and the main is the plat (PLAH). Dessert is the same word in both, and mignardises (meen-yar-DEEZ) are the small sweets served with coffee.

À la carte (ah lah KART) means from the card: every dish chosen and priced on its own. Prix fixe (pree FEEKS) means fixed price: a set run of courses for one price, often with a choice at each. Table d'hôte (tah-bluh DOHT), the host's table, began as an inn's meal at a set hour and price, and now means much the same. A tasting menu, dégustation (day-goos-tah-SYOHN), is a longer run of small courses chosen by the kitchen.

Jus (ZHOO) is the natural juice of a roast, often reduced, thinner than a sauce. A coulis (koo-LEE) is a smooth, sieved purée of fruit or vegetables used as a sauce, and a purée is anything blended smooth. A mousse is lightened with whipped cream or beaten egg white, sweet or savoury. Velouté (veh-loo-TAY), velvety, is a light stock of veal, chicken or fish thickened with a blond roux, and on many menus a smooth, creamy soup. Beurre (BURR) is butter and crème (KREM) is cream.

Confit (kohn-FEE), from the French for to preserve, is food cooked slowly in fat or syrup: classically duck legs cured with salt and cooked under fat until tender, then crisped; garlic or tomato confit is cooked slowly in oil, and fruit confit is preserved in sugar. Flambé (flahm-BAY) means flamed: spirit lit in a hot pan. En papillote (ahn pah-pee-YOHT) means sealed in a parcel and baked, so the food steams in its own juices. Meunière (muhn-YAIR), the miller's wife's way, is fish dusted in flour, cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley.

The common slips are easy to hear: jus said like juice, the h or s of hors sounded, with au jus, which says with twice, and entrée used without saying which end of the meal you mean. One habit mends them all: say the word once, then say what it is.

At Brennan's the entrées are main courses, listed after the starters, soups and salads. The Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper; ask at lineup, the short meeting before service, whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest of the steam. The two $80 tasting menus of the eightieth year are prix fixe: a set run of courses at one price. The Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit, and Bananas Foster is flambéed on the guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart.

Lead with the dish and let the French follow: the duck confit, a leg cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, then crisped. Never correct how a guest says a word; use your own way in your next sentence. When you do not know a word, ask the kitchen: a server who checks is trusted, and one who guesses is not.

faults.cause: Reading a French word as English, so jus becomes juice and the s of hors is said.
faults.fix: Learn the few dozen words aloud before service, with their respellings, and say them plainly.

faults.cause: Au already means with, so the phrase says with twice.
faults.fix: Say served au jus, or with its juice.

faults.cause: In France the word means a starter; on an American menu, a main course.
faults.fix: Say main course or starter as well, so the guest knows which end of the meal you mean.

faults.cause: The word was said and never explained.
faults.fix: Say the word once, then say what it is in plain English.

brennans.how: The Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, so the fish steams in its own juices. Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest about the steam.
The Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit: cured, cooked slowly under fat, then crisped. Describe the method in general and promise no house times.
Bananas Foster is flambéed at the table on the guéridon, the tableside cart: the spirit is lit in the pan and the flame dies before the dessert is plated.

The Traditional Breakfast, one of the two $80 tasting menus of the eightieth year, is a prix fixe: a set run of courses at one price, with the Eggs Hussarde among its courses. Read its pours from the printed card at lineup.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What do à la, au and aux, and en mean on a menu?
cards.back: À la means in the style of; au and aux mean with, one thing or several; en means in, as in en papillote.

cards.front: Why does entrée mean different things to an American guest and a French one?
cards.back: On an American menu it is the main course; in France today it is the starter, and the main course is the plat.

cards.front: What is an amuse-bouche, and does the guest order it?
cards.back: A single bite sent by the chef before the meal to wake the appetite. It is neither ordered nor charged.

cards.front: What does hors d'oeuvre mean, and how is it said?
cards.back: Literally outside the work: small savoury bites served apart from the meal, often with drinks. Say or DURV, with no h and no s.

cards.front: What are mignardises, and when do they come?
cards.back: The small sweets served with coffee at the very end of the meal, after dessert.

cards.front: How does prix fixe differ from à la carte?
cards.back: Prix fixe is a set run of courses for one price; à la carte means every dish is chosen and priced on its own.

cards.front: What do table d'hôte and a tasting menu mean today?
cards.back: Table d'hôte, the host's table, began as an inn's meal at a set hour and now means much the same as prix fixe. A tasting menu, or dégustation, is a longer run of small courses chosen by the kitchen.

cards.front: What is the difference between a jus and a coulis?
cards.back: A jus is the natural juice of a roast, often reduced; a coulis is a smooth, sieved purée of fruit or vegetables.

cards.front: What does confit mean on a menu?
cards.back: From the French for to preserve: classically duck legs salted and cooked slowly under fat until tender, crisped to serve; on menus garlic or tomato can be confit in oil, and fruit in sugar syrup.

cards.front: What does meunière promise on a fish?
cards.back: The miller's wife's way: fish dusted in flour, cooked in butter, finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley.

cards.front: What do en papillote and flambé mean on the Brennan's menu?
cards.back: En papillote: sealed in a parcel and baked; our Gulf Fish is wrapped in banana leaf, so warn of the steam. Flambé: flamed, spirit lit in a hot pan, as Bananas Foster is on the guéridon at the table.

cards.front: What is the habit for any French word at the table?
cards.back: Say the word once, simply, then say what it is in plain English. The French is there to help, never to impress.

questions.q: On a menu, what does au mean in a name such as au jus?
questions.answer: With
distractors: In
On
Without
questions.why: Au and aux mean with, one thing or several: au jus is with its juice, so with au jus says with twice.

questions.q: A guest from Paris asks for an entrée. What are they most likely asking for?
questions.answer: A starter
distractors: A main course
A dessert
A side dish
questions.why: In France today entrée means the first course; American menus kept the word for the main course.

questions.q: What is an amuse-bouche, as a menu uses the word?
questions.answer: One bite the chef sends before the meal
distractors: A small sweet served with coffee
A starter the guest orders to share
A palate cleanser between courses
questions.why: The amuse-bouche, a mouth amuser, comes unasked and is not charged; the sweets with coffee are mignardises.

questions.q: Which describes a prix fixe menu?
questions.answer: A set run of courses for one price
distractors: Every dish chosen and priced on its own
Dishes cooked at the guest's table
Dishes served family style for the table to share
questions.why: Prix fixe means fixed price; à la carte is the menu where every dish is priced on its own.

questions.q: What is a coulis, as a menu uses the word?
questions.answer: A smooth, sieved purée used as a sauce
distractors: The natural juice of a roast, often reduced
Butter whisked into a wine reduction
Cream thickened with egg yolk
questions.why: A coulis is fruit or vegetables puréed and sieved smooth; the natural juice of a roast is a jus.

questions.q: What does confit describe on a menu?
questions.answer: Classically, salted duck legs cooked slowly in fat
distractors: Meat flamed with spirit in a pan at the guest's table
Fish sealed in a paper parcel and baked in the oven
Fish floured and cooked in butter, then brown butter
questions.why: Confit, from the French for to preserve, classically means salted duck legs cooked slowly in fat until tender; garlic or tomato can be confit in oil, and fruit in sugar.

questions.q: A trout is served meunière. What should the guest expect?
questions.answer: Floured, cooked in butter, brown butter and lemon
distractors: Poached in white wine and served with peeled grapes
Sealed in a paper parcel and baked so it steams
Grilled over wood and served with a pepper sauce
questions.why: Meunière, the miller's wife's way, is named for the flour: the fish is dusted, cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley.

questions.q: What is the Brennan's Gulf Fish en Papillote wrapped in?
questions.answer: Banana leaf
distractors: Parchment paper
Puff pastry
Aluminium foil
questions.why: En papillote means in paper, but the house uses banana leaf, which holds the moisture in just as well.

questions.q: Bananas Foster is flambéed on the guéridon at Brennan's. What does flambé mean?
questions.answer: Flamed: spirit lit in a hot pan
distractors: Sealed in a parcel and baked
Cooked slowly under fat
Dusted in flour and cooked in butter
questions.why: Flambé means flamed: the spirit is lit in a hot pan at the table. Sealed and baked is en papillote, slow cooking under fat is confit, and flour and butter is meunière.

questions.q: A server describing the tasting menu reaches the word dégustation. What is the right habit?
questions.answer: Say the word, then explain it in plain English
distractors: Say the French twice, more slowly, so it sticks
Correct how the guest said the word earlier
Spell the word out so the guest can read it
questions.why: The French is there to help the guest choose, so say it simply and follow it at once with what it means.

entries.title: Mise en place words
entries.summary: The French names a classical kitchen uses for its pans, strainers, herb bundles, prep jobs and flavour bases. Read at sight, they turn a prep list into clear work: monder the tomatoes, a bouquet garni for the stock, duxelles for the filling.
entries.guest: Persillade is a fresh topping of chopped parsley and garlic; on our Creole Hanger Steak it comes with toasted pumpkin seeds for crunch.

paras: Mise en place (meez ahn PLAHS), everything in its place, is the cook's setting up before service, and it has an entry of its own; this one is its vocabulary. A classical kitchen names its pans, strainers, herb bundles, prep jobs and flavour bases in French, in short words made for speed. A sous chef writes the prep list in them and expects every cook to read it at sight.

Vessels first. A bain-marie (ban mah-REE) is a water bath for gentle heat, and also the tall steel pot that holds a sauce in it on the line. A sautoir (soh-TWAHR) is a straight-sided sauté pan that keeps a pan sauce in; a sauteuse (soh-TUHZ) has sloping sides for tossing and fast reduction. A rondeau (rohn-DOH) is wide and fairly shallow with two loop handles, for braising in quantity. A marmite (mar-MEET) is a tall lidded stockpot, a russe (ROOS) a long-handled saucepan, and a plaque (PLAHK) a flat baking tray.

Then the tools. A chinois (sheen-WAH) is a cone of fine mesh for straining sauces and stocks; American kitchens call the coarser perforated cone a china cap. A tamis (tah-MEE) is a drum sieve for pressing purées smooth. An étamine (ay-tah-MEEN) is a straining cloth of muslin or cheesecloth, for the clearest liquids. A mandoline (man-doh-LEEN) is a blade set in a frame for even slices, used with its guard every time. A spider is a wide wire skimmer for lifting food from oil or water.

Bundles carry flavour into a pot and come out again. A bouquet garni (boo-KAY gar-NEE) is parsley stalks, thyme and a bay leaf wrapped in leek green and tied, the string fastened to the handle so it lifts out. A sachet d'épices (sah-SHAY day-PEES) does the same for loose spice: peppercorns, bay, thyme and parsley stems knotted in cheesecloth. An oignon piqué (on-YOHN pee-KAY) is a peeled onion with a bay leaf pinned on by cloves, simmered in milk for béchamel, milk thickened with a roux. An oignon brûlé (on-YOHN broo-LAY) is a halved onion charred dark on the flat top, the griddle plate, for colour in brown stock and consommé, a clear soup of clarified stock.

The verbs name jobs. Monder (mohn-DAY) is to skin after a brief blanch: score a tomato, 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water, and the skin slips off. Blanchir (blahn-SHEER) is to blanch, a brief plunge into boiling water, often then into iced water. Dégorger (day-gor-ZHAY) is to draw out, soaking sweetbreads in cold water or salting cucumber. Dépouiller (day-poo-YAY) is to skim a simmering sauce. Réduire (ray-DWEER) is to reduce and passer (pah-SAY) to strain. Napper (nah-PAY) is to coat: a sauce à la nappe coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it. Monter (mohn-TAY) is to mount, whisking in cold butter or whipping whites or cream.

Mirepoix (meer-PWAH) is onion, carrot and celery, by the standard kitchen rule two parts onion to one of each other by weight; about 450 g (1 lb) flavours 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of stock, and it is strained out. For a fish fumet, a quick fish stock, or any stock or sauce that must stay ivory-pale, a white mirepoix swaps the carrot for leek and often mushroom trimmings; a classical white veal or chicken stock keeps its carrot, simply never browned.

A matignon (mah-tee-NYOHN) is an edible mirepoix, cut fine, with ham or without, stewed gently in butter and left in the dish. Duxelles (dook-SEL) is mushrooms and shallot chopped fine and cooked in butter until every drop of moisture has gone. Persillade (pair-see-YAHD) is chopped parsley and garlic, added at the last moment. Concassée (kon-ka-SAY) means roughly chopped: tomato concassée is peeled, seeded and diced.
Most slips are confusions: a sauteuse fetched for a sautoir's job spills its sauce, and a coarse cone where the list said étamine leaves a consommé cloudy.

At Brennan's, the Seafood Gumbo starts from the holy trinity, onion, celery and green bell pepper: Louisiana's mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, softened and left in the pot like a matignon. Creamed spinach classically begins with blanchir and a hard squeeze. The dinner Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade, with toasted pumpkin seeds.

A few of these words reach a menu: persillade on our Creole Hanger Steak, and duxelles on many classical ones. A server says the word, then what it is: chopped parsley and garlic; mushrooms chopped fine and cooked down in butter.

ratios.label: Mirepoix, by weight
ratios.value: 2 parts onion, 1 part carrot, 1 part celery

ratios.label: Mirepoix to stock
ratios.value: About 450 g (1 lb) for 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of finished stock

ratios.label: A classic bouquet garni
ratios.value: Parsley stalks, a sprig of thyme and a bay leaf, tied in leek green

ratios.label: Monder a tomato
ratios.value: 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then straight into iced water

faults.cause: A sauteuse fetched when the job needed a sautoir, whose straight sides hold liquid.
faults.fix: Learn the two by their sides: straight for a sautoir, sloping for a sauteuse.

faults.cause: Strained through a coarse cone, or pressed hard through the mesh.
faults.fix: Pass it through a fine chinois or an étamine, and let it run rather than forcing it.

faults.cause: Duxelles taken off the heat while still wet.
faults.fix: Cook until the pan is dry and the paste pulls together, then cool it before use.

faults.cause: Left too long in the boiling water when monder only needed seconds.
faults.fix: Count 10 to 15 seconds, then go straight into iced water.

faults.cause: A bouquet garni tied loosely, or a sachet that split.
faults.fix: Tie it tight with string, tie the end to the handle, and lift it out whole.

brennans.how: The gumbo starts from the holy trinity, onion, celery and green bell pepper softened together: Louisiana's mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot. Unlike a stock's mirepoix, it is never strained out.

Creamed spinach classically begins with blanchir: blanched, plunged into iced water, squeezed hard and chopped, then bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg. Confirm the house method with the kitchen.
The Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade: the French parsley and garlic finish, thrown on at the last second, with toasted pumpkin seeds for crunch.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What is the difference between a sautoir and a sauteuse?
cards.back: A sautoir has straight sides that hold a pan sauce; a sauteuse has sloping sides for tossing and fast reduction.

cards.front: What two things can bain-marie mean in a kitchen?
cards.back: A water bath for gentle heat, and the tall steel pot that holds a sauce in that bath on the line.

cards.front: What are a rondeau and a marmite used for?
cards.back: A rondeau is wide and fairly shallow with two loop handles, for braising and searing in quantity; a marmite is a tall lidded stockpot.

cards.front: What is each for: the chinois, the tamis and the étamine?
cards.back: The chinois, a fine mesh cone, strains sauces and stocks; the tamis, a drum sieve, presses purées smooth; the étamine, a cloth, gives the clearest liquid.

cards.front: What goes into a classic bouquet garni, and why is it tied?
cards.back: Parsley stalks, thyme and a bay leaf in leek green, tied with string so the whole bundle lifts out of the pot.

cards.front: What is the difference between an oignon piqué and an oignon brûlé?
cards.back: Piqué is an onion with a bay leaf pinned on by cloves, for béchamel; brûlé is a halved onion charred dark, for colour in consommé and brown stock.

cards.front: What does monder mean, and how is it done to a tomato?
cards.back: To skin after a brief blanch: score it, 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water, and the skin slips off.

cards.front: What does dégorger mean?
cards.back: To draw something out: soaking sweetbreads in cold water to clear blood, or salting cucumber to pull out its water.

cards.front: What does dépouiller mean at the stove?
cards.back: To skim the fat and scum from a simmering sauce or stock, so it ends clear and clean tasting.

cards.front: What does napper mean, and how do you test it?
cards.back: To coat. A sauce at nappe coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line drawn through it with a finger.

cards.front: How does a matignon differ from a mirepoix?
cards.back: Mirepoix is rough-cut onion, carrot and celery, two to one to one, strained out; matignon is cut fine, stewed in butter and left in the dish.

cards.front: What are duxelles and persillade?
cards.back: Duxelles: mushrooms and shallot chopped fine, cooked in butter until every drop of moisture has gone and the paste pulls together. Persillade: chopped parsley and garlic, added at the last moment.

questions.q: The sous chef calls for a sautoir to finish a pan sauce. What do you bring?
questions.answer: A straight-sided sauté pan
distractors: A sloping-sided sauté pan
A wide two-handled braising pan
A tall lidded stockpot
questions.why: A sautoir's straight sides hold a pan sauce; the sloping sauteuse is for tossing, the rondeau braises in quantity and the marmite makes stock.

questions.q: Which of these strains a consommé clearest?
questions.answer: An étamine
distractors: A china cap
A tamis
A colander
questions.why: An étamine is a cloth of muslin or cheesecloth, finer than any mesh, so it holds back what a cone, a drum sieve or a colander lets through.

questions.q: Why is a bouquet garni tied with string, the end fastened to the handle?
questions.answer: So it lifts out whole once its flavour is in
distractors: So it holds the herbs below the surface
So the leek green cooks evenly with it
So the cook can tell when it is done
questions.why: The bundle carries flavour into the pot and must come out again; tied and fastened, it leaves no loose herbs to strain out.

questions.q: Which bundle is the classical one for the milk of a béchamel?
questions.answer: An oignon piqué
distractors: An oignon brûlé
A bouquet garni
A sachet d'épices
questions.why: The oignon piqué, an onion with a bay leaf pinned on by cloves, is simmered in the milk; the brûlé colours brown stock, and the bouquet and sachet flavour stocks and braises.

questions.q: A prep list says monder the tomatoes. What do you do?
questions.answer: Blanch them briefly and slip off the skins
distractors: Roast them in a hot oven until they collapse
Salt them to draw out their water
Chop them roughly with their skins on
questions.why: Monder is to skin after a brief blanch: 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water, and the skin slips off.

questions.q: What is a cook doing when told to dépouiller the sauce?
questions.answer: Skimming fat and scum from its surface
distractors: Whisking cold butter into it off the heat
Coating the plate with it before service
Straining it through a cloth into a pan
questions.why: Dépouiller is skimming; mounting with butter is monter, coating is napper and straining is passer.

questions.q: How do you know a sauce has reached nappe?
questions.answer: It coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it
distractors: It sets firm in the fridge when it is chilled overnight
It runs straight off the spoon like water
It forms stiff peaks when it is whisked hard
questions.why: Napper means to coat: a sauce at nappe clings to the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line.

questions.q: What is the standard proportion of a mirepoix by weight?
questions.answer: Two parts onion, one carrot, one celery
distractors: Equal parts onion, carrot and celery
Two parts carrot, one onion, one leek
Two parts celery, one onion, one carrot
questions.why: Onion leads at half the weight, with carrot and celery a quarter each; the mix is cut to suit the cooking time and strained out.

questions.q: Duxelles for a pastry filling is taken off the heat too soon. What goes wrong?
questions.answer: The wet paste makes the pastry soggy
distractors: The mushrooms turn bitter and black
The shallot stays raw and sharp
The butter sets hard in the filling
questions.why: Duxelles is cooked until every drop of moisture has gone; any water left behind soaks into the pastry around it.

questions.q: Our dinner Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade. What is a persillade?
questions.answer: Chopped parsley and garlic, added at the end
distractors: Mushrooms and shallot cooked dry in butter
Peeled, seeded and diced tomato
Onion, carrot and celery cut fine
questions.why: Persillade, from persil, parsley, is chopped parsley and garlic thrown on at the last moment; duxelles is the mushroom paste, concassée the tomato and matignon the fine-cut vegetables.

entries.title: The cuts by name
entries.say: As it reads: the cuts by name.
entries.summary: The French names for the classical cuts: strips, dice, slices and shapes, from julienne to tourné, and the garnish names that promise a cut. Each name is a promise of shape, on a prep list and on a menu.
entries.guest: Our Brabant potatoes are cubed and fried golden, then tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; a pavé is thin potato layers pressed into a neat brick and seared.

paras: Each classical cut carries a French name, and the name is a promise of shape. Julienne means fine strips, brunoise tiny dice, tourné a seven-sided barrel. A prep list written in these names tells a cook exactly what to cut, and a menu that uses them tells a guest what will be on the plate. This entry is the vocabulary, what each name means and how to say it; the knife work and the exact measures belong to Knife cuts.

The strips run from fine to thick. Julienne (zhoo-lee-EN) is the finest, a thin matchstick that cooks in moments or sits raw in a salad. Allumette (ah-loo-MET), a match, is about the size of julienne or a touch thicker, and mostly a potato word, for fries cut thin. Bâtonnet (bah-toh-NAY), a little stick, is thicker and square, the strip a cook cuts on the way to a dice. Pont-neuf (pohn NUHF) is the thick potato stick fried as a chunky chip, often stacked like logs.

A dice is a strip cut across into cubes, so each strip has its dice. Julienne cut across gives brunoise (broon-WAHZ), the finest dice, for the end of a sauce or to garnish a consommé, a clear soup. Bâtonnet gives macédoine (mah-say-DWAHN), a small, even dice. A thicker stick gives parmentier (par-mahn-TYAY), a larger cube, classically of potato. Mirepoix (meer-PWAH) is the exception: a rough cut, sized to how long it will cook and strained out at the end, so nobody cuts it to an exact size.

Paysanne (pay-ee-ZAHN), country style, is thin, flat pieces that keep the outline of the vegetable, squares, rounds or triangles, for soup. A rondelle (rohn-DEL) is a round cut straight across a carrot or cucumber. Émincé (ay-man-SAY) means thinly sliced; on a menu, an émincé is thin strips of meat. A chiffonade (shif-uh-NAHD) is leaves rolled and sliced into fine ribbons. Ciseler (seez-LAY) is to chop an onion or shallot very fine, slicing one way and then across, so it falls into tiny even pieces without being crushed. A tourné (toor-NAY), turned, is a barrel with seven faces and flat ends. Parisienne (pah-ree-ZYEN) means balls scooped with a melon baller.

Some garnish names promise a cut. Jardinière (zhar-dee-NYAIR), from the garden, means vegetables in bâtonnets, carrots and turnips with peas and French beans. Printanière (pran-tah-NYAIR), spring, means young vegetables cut small or turned at the start of their season. Macédoine is both a cut and a dish: a mix of diced vegetables, or of fruit, cut to that small dice.

Two names honour a man and a bridge. Parmentier is Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the pharmacist who campaigned for the potato in eighteenth-century France, which is why his name means potato on a menu. Pont-neuf is usually linked to the Pont Neuf in Paris, where street sellers are said to have fried potatoes. Where julienne came from, nobody has proved.

On the line, the name means the house size: a chef who asks for brunoise shallots means the brunoise this kitchen cuts, so if you are unsure, cut a few and show them before you cut the lot. On the floor, say the name and then the shape in plain words: a julienne of vegetables is fine matchsticks, a chiffonade of basil is fine ribbons, pommes parisiennes are little potato balls.

On the Brennan's menus the potatoes carry the lesson. Brabant potatoes are cubed, blanched or par-fried, then fried golden and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup, the short meeting before service. The smoked potato pavé on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is named for its shape: pavé is French for paving stone, and a pavé is classically potato sliced paper-thin, layered, pressed, cut into bricks and seared; the house's own method is the kitchen's detail.

faults.cause: A plain dice cut where the list said brunoise.
faults.fix: Read the name as a shape and size; when unsure, cut a few and show the chef first.

faults.cause: Paysanne cut thick or in pieces of different sizes.
faults.fix: Keep paysanne thin and even, following the outline of the vegetable.

faults.fault: A chiffonade blackened at the edges
faults.cause: Cut long before service, or with a dull knife that bruises the leaves.
faults.fix: Cut it with a sharp knife at the last moment.

faults.fault: A cloudy stock full of shreds
faults.cause: Mirepoix cut fine for a stock that simmers for hours.
faults.fix: Size the mirepoix to the cooking time: large for a long stock, small for a quick sauce.

brennans.how: Brabant potatoes are cubed, blanched or par-fried, then fried golden and crisp and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley. Confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup.

Pavé means paving stone, for its neat rectangular block of thin potato layers, cut into bricks and seared until each face is crisp. The house method, and where the smoke comes in, are the kitchen's detail.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What does julienne mean?
cards.back: Fine strips, thin as a matchstick or thinner, that cook in moments or sit raw in a salad.

cards.front: Name the four classical strips, from fine to thick.
cards.back: Julienne and allumette, much the same size, then bâtonnet and pont-neuf: allumette and pont-neuf are mostly potato words, for thin fries and thick chips.

cards.front: What is brunoise, and which strip is it cut from?
cards.back: The finest dice, cut across a julienne, for a consommé garnish or the finish of a sauce.

cards.front: How do macédoine and parmentier differ?
cards.back: Macédoine is a small, even dice cut from bâtonnet; parmentier is a larger cube, classically of potato.

cards.front: Why is mirepoix not cut to an exact size like the other dice?
cards.back: It is a rough cut, sized to how long it will cook and strained out at the end: large for a long stock, so it lasts without breaking down, small for a quick sauce.

cards.front: What does paysanne mean as a cut?
cards.back: Country style: thin, flat pieces that keep the outline of the vegetable, squares, rounds or triangles, for soup.

cards.front: What is a chiffonade?
cards.back: Leaves such as basil, stacked, rolled and sliced into fine ribbons, cut at the last moment so they stay green.

cards.front: What does ciseler mean for an onion or shallot?
cards.back: To chop it very fine, slicing one way and then across, so it falls into tiny even pieces without being crushed.

cards.front: What shape is a tourné?
cards.back: Turned: a small barrel with seven faces and flat ends, carved from potato or a root vegetable.

cards.front: What does parisienne mean as a cut?
cards.back: Balls scooped with a melon baller, as in pommes parisiennes, little potato balls.

cards.front: What cut does a jardinière garnish promise, and what does printanière promise?
cards.back: Jardinière, from the garden, is vegetables in bâtonnets; printanière, spring, is young vegetables cut small or turned.

cards.front: Why is the smoked potato pavé on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak called a pavé?
cards.back: Pavé means paving stone: thin potato slices are layered, pressed and cut into neat bricks, then seared. How ours is smoked is the kitchen's detail.

questions.q: A prep list asks for brunoise carrots. What do you cut?
questions.answer: The finest dice, cut across a julienne
distractors: Thick sticks cut for the fryer
Thin rounds cut across the carrot
Rough chunks sized for a long stock
questions.why: Brunoise is julienne cut across into tiny cubes; thick sticks are pont-neuf, rounds are rondelles and rough chunks are mirepoix.

questions.q: Which of these strips is the thickest?
questions.answer: Pont-neuf
distractors: Julienne
Allumette
Bâtonnet
questions.why: The strips run julienne and allumette, much the same size, then bâtonnet and pont-neuf, the thick potato stick fried as a chunky chip.

questions.q: As a cut, what is parmentier?
questions.answer: A larger cube, classically of potato
distractors: The finest dice, cut across a julienne
A small, even dice cut from bâtonnet
Thin, flat pieces that keep the outline
questions.why: Parmentier is the larger dice, classically of potato; brunoise is the finest, macédoine the small dice and paysanne the flat country cut.

questions.q: Basil is stacked, rolled and sliced into fine ribbons. What is the cut called?
questions.answer: Chiffonade
distractors: Paysanne
Émincé
Parisienne
questions.why: Chiffonade is the ribbon cut for leaves; paysanne is thin flat pieces, émincé thin slices and parisienne scooped balls.

questions.q: How many faces does a classical tourné have?
questions.answer: Seven
distractors: Four
Five
Nine
questions.why: The classical tourné has seven faces and flat ends; cutting every piece to that one standard makes them match on the plate and cook at the same rate.

questions.q: What does ciseler mean when a chef asks for it with shallots?
questions.answer: Chop them very fine, never crushed
distractors: Slice them into thin, even rounds
Cut them into fine, even strips
Crush them to a paste with salt
questions.why: Ciseler slices the shallot one way and then across, so it falls into tiny even pieces rather than being crushed into juice.

questions.q: A dish is served with a jardinière garnish. What cut should the vegetables be?
questions.answer: Bâtonnets
distractors: Fine ribbons
Scooped balls
Paper-thin slices
questions.why: Jardinière, from the garden, promises vegetables cut in bâtonnets, usually carrots and turnips with peas and French beans.

questions.q: Why is a mirepoix for a long stock cut large?
questions.answer: It must last the cooking without breaking down
distractors: It must look neat and even on the finished plate
It must soften fully within a minute or two
It must pass through the chinois with the stock
questions.why: Mirepoix is sized to its cooking time and strained out; cut fine for a long simmer it breaks down and clouds the stock.

entries.title: Cooking terms on the ticket
entries.say: As it reads: cooking terms on the ticket.
entries.summary: The words that carry an order from the table to the kitchen: doneness in French and English, egg orders, modifiers such as no, add, sub and on the side, seat numbers, and an allergy written down and said to the kitchen.
entries.guest: How would you like the filet cooked? Medium rare has a warm red centre; medium is pink in the centre, with a little less juice.

paras: A ticket is the order as the kitchen reads it: each dish, how it is cooked, what changes and which seat it goes to. Its words are short and fixed, so nothing is misread. Write it well and the kitchen has everything at once; write it badly and back comes a steak or a plate nobody can place.

Doneness, called temperature on the floor, is the first thing a ticket carries for meat. French kitchens use four words. Bleu (BLUH) is seared hard outside and barely warmed within. Saignant (sen-YAHN), bleeding, is rare: red and juicy at the centre. À point (ah PWAN), at the point, is pink through, roughly medium rare to medium. Bien cuit (byan KWEE) is well done. American kitchens use five steps, rare, medium rare, medium, medium well and well done. Roughly, at the centre after resting: rare about 52°C (126°F), medium rare 57°C (135°F), medium 60 to 63°C (140 to 145°F), medium well 65°C (149°F), well done 71°C (160°F) or more.

The two ladders do not line up. The French count four steps to the American five, so à point covers what an American kitchen splits into medium rare and medium, and French cooking leans rarer: a guest who says à point may mean either. Translate by colour, not by word: ask what the guest wants to see at the centre, red, pink or none, and write the house word for it. Each kitchen sets its own marks. The USDA recommends 63°C (145°F) and a three-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, and menus that serve meat less cooked print a consumer advisory, as the FDA Food Code asks.

Egg orders name what the guest will see. Poached is cooked out of the shell in water, white set and yolk running. Sunny side up is fried on one side only, never turned, the yolk liquid. Over easy is fried and turned briefly, the yolk still runny; over medium and over hard cook it further. Soft-boiled is simmered in the shell so the yolk stays soft. Soft scrambled is stirred gently into moist, creamy curds. How each is cooked belongs to the egg station; the ticket's job is to say which, exactly.

Modifiers change a dish. On the side means a sauce or dressing served apart. No takes something off; add puts something on, often at a charge; sub swaps one thing for another, only when the kitchen allows it. Rush means the table needs it fast, and VIP marks a guest the house wants looked after with extra care. Hold means wait until fire, which means cook it now; since some kitchens also use hold for leave off, write no for anything taken away. À la minute (ah lah mee-NOOT) means cooked to order at that moment, against made ahead, prepared earlier and finished to order.

Seat numbers place each plate. Every table has a seat one, fixed by house rule from a landmark such as the door or the window, and the rest follow round the table in one direction. Each order is written against its seat, so the runner can set every plate before the right guest without asking who had what.

An allergy goes on the ticket and to the kitchen by voice, every time. Write it as the system flags it, then tell the chef or the expediter, and the captain, in person. The ticket carries the order through service; the spoken word makes sure a person has heard it. The kitchen, not the server, decides what a dish can do, so promise nothing until it has cleared the order.

At Brennan's the filet on the Traditional Breakfast has its temperature taken with the order. The poached eggs on the Eggs Hussarde come soft unless the guest asks otherwise; check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs. Egg Any Style is one egg in the guest's style, written exactly; confirm the styles offered at lineup, the short meeting before service. Whether the Chateaubriand for two can go out at two temperatures is a lineup question, not a promise. Restrictions are noted at the reservation, written on the ticket and cleared by the kitchen.

Well done, bien cuit, a rough guide

faults.fault: A steak sent back for doneness
faults.cause: A French or vague word went on the ticket, or nobody asked what colour the guest wanted.
faults.fix: Ask what the guest wants to see at the centre and write the house word for it.

faults.fault: Onions on a plate marked hold
faults.cause: In this kitchen hold means wait, not leave off.
faults.fix: Write no for anything taken away, and keep hold for timing.
Write every order against its seat, counted from the house's seat one.

faults.fault: An allergy on the ticket that the kitchen never heard spoken
faults.cause: The note was written but not said.
faults.fix: Say it to the chef or expediter and the captain as well, and let the kitchen clear the order.

faults.fault: A swap promised that the kitchen will not make
faults.cause: A sub offered at the table before anyone asked the kitchen.
faults.fix: Ask first, then offer; the kitchen decides what a dish can do.

brennans.how: Egg Any Style is one egg cooked as the guest asks: sunny side up, over easy, over medium, over hard, scrambled soft or firm, poached or soft-boiled. Write the style exactly, and confirm the styles offered at lineup.
The eggs on the Eggs Hussarde come soft poached, white set and yolk running, unless the guest asks otherwise. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs.
The Rohan duck breast on the dinner tasting is served pink, usually medium rare to medium. Confirm the kitchen's temperature at lineup before describing it to a guest.

cards.front: Give the four French doneness words in order, from least cooked to most.
cards.back: Bleu, very rare; saignant, rare; à point, pink through, roughly medium rare to medium; bien cuit, well done.

cards.front: Why do French à point and American medium rare not quite line up?
cards.back: France counts four steps to America's five, so à point spans medium rare and medium, and French cooking leans rarer. Ask what colour the guest wants at the centre.

cards.front: How do you take a doneness order from a guest who uses the French word?
cards.back: Translate by colour: ask what they want to see at the centre, red, pink or none, and write the house word for it.

cards.front: Roughly what centre temperatures do rare, medium rare and medium mean?
cards.back: About 52°C (126°F), 57°C (135°F) and 60 to 63°C (140 to 145°F) after resting, though each kitchen sets its own.

cards.front: What is the difference between sunny side up and over easy?
cards.back: Sunny side up is fried on one side and never turned; over easy is turned briefly, and the yolk stays runny in both.

cards.front: What do no, add and sub mean on a ticket?
cards.back: No takes something off, add puts something on, often at a charge, and sub swaps one thing for another when the kitchen allows.

cards.front: Why should a server write no rather than hold to take an item off?
cards.back: In many kitchens hold means wait, do not start the course yet, so hold the onions can leave the onions on.

cards.front: What does à la minute mean, against made ahead?
cards.back: Cooked to order at that moment; made ahead is prepared earlier and finished to order, so it is quicker but harder to change.

cards.front: Why is every order written against a seat number?
cards.back: So the runner can set each plate before the right guest without asking, counted round the table from the house's seat one.

cards.front: How does a guest's allergy reach the kitchen?
cards.back: Written on the ticket as the system flags it, and said in person to the chef or expediter and the captain; the kitchen clears the order.

cards.front: On the Brennan's Traditional Breakfast, when is the filet temperature taken?
cards.back: With the order, at the start, so the Petite Filet Mignon course can be cooked as the guest wants it.

cards.front: How do the poached eggs on the Eggs Hussarde come, unless the guest asks otherwise?
cards.back: Soft poached, white set and yolk running. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs.

questions.q: A guest orders a steak saignant. Which American word is closest?
questions.answer: Rare
distractors: Medium
Medium well
Well done
questions.why: Saignant means bleeding: red and juicy at the centre, the French word for rare.

questions.q: A French guest orders a steak à point and the server writes medium. Why might it arrive more done than the guest wanted?
questions.answer: À point is often pinker than an American medium
distractors: À point is the French word for well done
French kitchens count five steps to the American four
An American medium is rarer than à point
questions.why: France counts four steps to America's five, so à point spans medium rare and medium, and French cooking leans rarer than an American medium.

questions.q: What is the surest way to take a doneness order across the two languages?
questions.answer: Ask what colour they want at the centre
distractors: Write the guest's French word on the ticket
Always write medium rare
Let the kitchen choose for them
questions.why: Red, pink or none means the same in both kitchens; the server then writes the house word for that colour.

questions.q: Roughly what centre temperature, after resting, does a medium rare steak reach?
questions.why: Medium rare sits around 57°C (135°F); rare is nearer 52°C (126°F), medium 60 to 63°C (140 to 145°F) and well done 71°C (160°F) or more, and each kitchen sets its own marks.

questions.q: Which egg order is fried on one side only and never turned?
questions.answer: Sunny side up
distractors: Over easy
Over hard
Soft scrambled
questions.why: Sunny side up is never turned, so the yolk stays liquid under a set white; over easy is turned briefly.

questions.q: A guest wants no onions. Why write no onion rather than hold onion?
questions.answer: Hold can mean wait, not leave off
distractors: Hold means serve it on the side
Hold is charged as an extra
Hold is only for drinks orders
questions.why: In many kitchens hold is a timing word, so hold onion can be read as wait; no is never misread.

questions.q: What does writing seat numbers on a ticket let the runner do?
questions.answer: Set each plate before the right guest
distractors: Fire the next course before the table is ready
Skip the check of each plate at the pass
Split the bill and charge each guest separately
questions.why: Each order is written against its seat, counted from the house's seat one, so nobody has to ask who had the fish.

questions.q: When a guest names an allergy, what should reach the kitchen?
questions.answer: The ticket flag and your spoken word
distractors: The flag on the ticket, with nothing said
Your spoken word, with nothing on the ticket
A note on the guest's bill for the captain
questions.why: The ticket carries it through service and the spoken word makes sure a person heard it; the kitchen then clears the order.

questions.q: On the Brennan's Traditional Breakfast, when does the server take the filet temperature?
questions.answer: With the order
distractors: When the filet course is fired
After the eggs are cleared
When the guest asks for it
questions.why: The house guidance is to take the filet temperature with the order, so the course is cooked as the guest wants it.
